source: Camposampiero et al. (2025) Can Large Reasoning Models do Analogical Reasoning under Perceptual Uncertainty?
finding: Reasoning models fail Raven-style analogical rule induction when inputs are long, wide-range and noisy. Gap 4.
numbers: o3-mini: 86.6% on I-RAVEN to 17.0% on I-RAVEN-X with perceptual uncertainty (chance 12.5%), using 3.4x more reasoning tokens. DeepSeek R1: 80.6% to 23.2%. Neuro-symbolic ARLC: 98.6% to 88.0%.
limits: Matrix tasks with symbolic attributes, not Duncker-style problem analogy. Perception noise is simulated.
agent_relevance: Extra thinking tokens do not rescue a model whose input representation is noisy. Do not assume O7 improves by thinking longer.

source: Camposampiero et al. (2025) Can Large Reasoning Models do Analogical Reasoning under Perceptual Uncertainty?
finding: Reasoning-token cost grows with difficulty, and more effort gives no gain on the hardest setting. Gap 4.
numbers: o3-mini tokens went from 7,209 (base) to 18,589 in the hardest setting. High effort (up to 100,000 tokens, 2.7x) gave +6% on I-RAVEN but 0 on I-RAVEN-X; with all uncertainty on, high effort reached only 31.0% at 53,596 tokens.
limits: One model family, one task type.
agent_relevance: Cap analogue-mapping effort; prefer an external check (code or constraint check) over longer reasoning.

source: Camposampiero et al. (2025) Can Large Reasoning Models do Analogical Reasoning under Perceptual Uncertainty?
finding: Reasoning models handle longer rules and wider ranges far better than plain LLMs, so the collapse is about uncertainty, not length. Gap 4.
numbers: Plain LLMs fall to near 0% arithmetic accuracy on I-RAVEN-X; reasoning models lose much less. Authors attribute 5.6% of o3-mini's drop to length/range and most of the rest to perceptual uncertainty (R1 even gained 2.2% from length).
limits: GPT-4 and Llama-3 numbers taken from an earlier paper.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models map well on clean input; noise in the source or target description is the weak point.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Authors' reply: GPT-4 with code execution solves the shuffled-alphabet letter-string analogy at human level. Gap 5.
numbers: Human N=99 (interval 1) and N=97 (interval 2). GPT-4 vs humans P=8.9e-13; GPT-4 + code execution vs humans P=0.496 (no difference). Interval-size effect for GPT-4 + code P=0.066.
limits: Written by the authors of the original claim. Code use was spontaneous. Code route is not how humans do it.
agent_relevance: Supports the view that the failure is index counting, not missing abstraction. An agent with a code tool can close this gap.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: GPT-4 errors on the shuffled alphabet are often a valid alternative rule, like human errors. Gap 5.
numbers: 46% of GPT-4 errors used a valid alternative rule vs 39% of human errors (human figure from Lewis and Mitchell). GPT-3 also beat humans on the novel Digit Matrices, which use a reordered digit sequence.
agent_relevance: Score answers that follow a valid alternative rule separately; single-answer scoring understates analogy skill.

source: Hodel and West (2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Counterfactual letter-string tests: GPT-3 collapses on a synthetic alphabet while humans hold. Gap 5.
numbers: GPT-3 generative accuracy under 0.1 on extend-sequence, successor/predecessor and fix-alphabetic-sequence with the synthetic alphabet; similar to original only on remove-redundant-letter and sort (2 of 6 types). Humans stayed consistently high across modifications.
limits: GPT-3 only; small mixed human sample.
agent_relevance: The failure is real, but with the Webb reply it looks like a counting/indexing failure (see d04).

source: Hodel and West (2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Hodel and West argue human tests may not measure the same thing in an LLM and training-data overlap cannot be ruled out. Gap 9.
numbers: They note the original authors admitted in peer review that some letter-string items could appear online. No new numbers beyond the GPT-3 counterexamples.
limits: Argument paper with a small appendix.
agent_relevance: Use fresh, generated items and permutations when testing O7; do not trust a public benchmark alone.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning (J Memory and Language 145)
finding: With semantic words mapped to symbol strings, best LLMs match humans in the default condition. Gap 5.
numbers: Defaults: GPT-4 (p=0.097), Claude 3 (p=0.194), Llama-405B (p=0.097) do not differ significantly from humans. Smaller models fail: Pythia-12B 0.0, Falcon-40B 0.1, GPT-3 0.5, Claude 2 0.6 reference match. Study 2: best LLM equals humans in all conditions and beats them on compositional variants.
limits: Reference-match scoring, not accuracy. Task is linguistic-to-nonlinguistic re-representation.
agent_relevance: A strong modern model can induce a relational rule across domains; skill scales with model quality.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning (J Memory and Language 145)
finding: LLMs are order-sensitive where humans are not. Gap 9.
numbers: Permuted Pairs drop: Claude 3 coef -1.78, GPT-4 -1.68, Llama-405B -2.34 (all p<0.001); humans unaffected. Distractor condition cost about 0.25 for all four subject types.
limits: Only the best three models analysed in detail.
agent_relevance: Shuffle example order and test each analogy twice; an order-dependent answer is not a stable mapping.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning (J Memory and Language 145)
finding: Models and humans differ in how they use the semantic structure of the source. Gap 3.
numbers: Only-RHS: Claude 3 and humans about 0.8, GPT-4 about 0.9, Llama about 0.5. Random Finals (one misleading item): humans about -0.5, Claude 3 -0.5, GPT-4 -0.8, Llama -0.4; models do not fall back to the simple right-hand-side strategy when the left side is uninformative.
limits: Different mechanisms are inferred, not shown.
agent_relevance: LLMs trust a source even when it is uninformative; a step asking 'is the source informative at all?' is worth testing.

source: Yu, Ying, He (2024) Thought Propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning with LLMs (ICLR)
finding: Thought Propagation (solve analogous problems, then refine the first answer) beats CoT for weak and mid models on shortest path; little room with GPT-4. Gap 1 and 2.
numbers: Optimal rate 0-shot: GPT-3.5 IO 0.33, CoT 0.26, TP 0.65; PaLM-2 IO 0.14, CoT 0.24, TP 0.36; GPT-4 IO 0.78, CoT 0.76, TP 0.88. TP also lowers over-length (GPT-3.5 0.12 vs 0.17 IO).
limits: Graph tasks with model-generated analogues; token cost not matched; authors' own benchmark.
agent_relevance: Large gain at GPT-3.5, +10 points at GPT-4 on synthetic tasks. No equal-token or real-problem test, so Gap 1 stays open.

source: Yu, Ying, He (2024) Thought Propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning with LLMs (ICLR)
finding: One layer of analogous-problem propagation gives most of the gain; a second layer adds little. Gap 2.
numbers: Authors state 1-layer TP is a big gain over 0-layer (IO); 2-layer TP is best but the extra gain is marginal. GPT-3.5 1-shot TP 0.74 vs IO 0.62; 5-shot TP 0.73 vs IO 0.61.
limits: Number of analogues per layer not equated with the human two-case design.
agent_relevance: Weak hint that one round of analogue use is enough for LLMs; no direct two-analogue schema test exists.

source: Yu, Ying, He (2024) Thought Propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning with LLMs (ICLR)
finding: Agent planning gains reported on ALFWorld from reusing analogous solved plans. Gap 1.
numbers: Paper reports large completion-rate gains over Reflexion-style and ReAct baselines (GPT-3 agent, 134 environments, 6 trials); exact table values were not extracted this session.

source: Hu and Frank (2024) Auxiliary task demands mask the capabilities of smaller language models (COLM)
finding: Method of asking changes measured analogy skill: production vs forced choice on digit matrices. Gap 5 and 9.
numbers: Significant model-size by evaluation-method interaction for analogical reasoning (z=2.631, p=0.009); the demand gap is largest for smaller models. OLMo 7B checkpoints: slower early improvement under the production method (interaction z=2.639, p=0.008, pooled with word prediction).
limits: Digit matrices only; small open models.
agent_relevance: A model may hold the skill yet fail an awkward output format. Test O7 with the lowest-demand format first.

source: Hu and Frank (2024) Auxiliary task demands mask the capabilities of smaller language models (COLM)
finding: Task-demand account partly resolves the Webb versus Lewis-Mitchell dispute but is not a full answer. Gap 5.
numbers: Reading across d04, d05, d06 and d14: failure on counterfactual alphabets tracks counting/indexing and answer format, and eases with tools or low-demand formats. Not shown anywhere: that models retrieve the right analogue unaided.
limits: Synthesis across papers, not one experiment.
agent_relevance: Separate mapping skill from retrieval skill in all agent tests.
